content:
On 9 August this year, the Hong Kong Observatory recorded its highest temperature ever of 36.9°C since records began in 1884, with Sheung Shui reaching an even higher 39.8°C in the mid-afternoon. In the scorching heat, I hid inside a long-shaped house, leaving only a narrow gap in the window for ventilation. In extreme heat, hot air really does rush indoors. So the balcony door and the hall windows were all shut. I live on the middle floor of a house nestled between two small hills, shielded from the sun on all sides except at noon. Even without air conditioning, three ceiling fans whirred through their creaking rhythm, spinning cool air around. Amid Hong Kong-style heatwaves, I have much to be grateful for.

Under the highest temperatures on record, I stayed home doing laundry. Just after 1 p.m., I washed two large bedsheets and duvet covers, four pairs of jeans, and a pile of T-shirts. Two hours later, I turned the bedsheets and covers over to dry on the other side. The result? Just after 6 p.m., I held the warm laundry—freshly as if just pulled from a big machine at the laundromat—and placed it on the bed. It felt as though I had not experienced such naturally sun-dried, clean laundry in ages. I ought to have been worrying for friends under the ferocious sun; only by washing load after load could I offset, just a little, the dreadfulness of that blazing heat.

August has become a nightmare. I do not know how many trips it will take to break free from that recurring summer of partings. In a night's dream, I strutted proudly, twisting my mother along as I walked, saying: 'My little mummy.' I gripped her tightly with joy. Then, I saw ahead a mysterious woman draped in a long, deep maroon cloak. Subconsciously, I did not want to see her face clearly, but eventually, the dream's camera kept zooming in on her face—she was a strange woman I did not recognise. Until I woke, a feeling of ecstatic abandon surfaced, and what I recalled was: I had dreamed of my mother again.

On the evening of 10 August 2020, our family sang hymns, kissed my mother's forehead, and said goodbye to her—that was a complete full stop. Yet learning to let go is a lifelong lesson. The unwillingness to part is a quiet wound. Six years on, there remain countless small regrets in the tiniest details, and in my mind I repeatedly rehearse the days that led to that one.

The regrets and reluctance of parting, sooner or later, regardless of age, will appear at different stages of life. A student in the writing class wrote about her late grandmother in her piece. It was a recollection, a mourning, a regret. When she was even younger, she had resented living with her grandmother in the countryside, spending her days full of little-monster energy bickering with her grandmother. Grandmother would pinch her ear; she would strike back, letting grandmother feel the pain she herself had felt. Then, through a crack in the door, the little girl saw her frail grandmother secretly wipe away tears. That very night, the girl fell ill with a fever, and walked blankly to her grandmother and said: 'I feel awful.'

To feel awful simply means being unwell—it is a child's way of describing illness. She had a high fever, her whole body burning hot. Without a word, grandmother found clean clothes for her to change into and immediately carried her on her back to the hospital to wait. That medicated oil scent, once despised, vaguely carried her all the way to the hospital. Shortly after, somehow, the scent vanished, and the little girl sat alone near the reception desk waiting. Then, several adults asked her: 'Where are your family?' As she spoke, she began to cry, until the medicated oil scent drifted near again, and she settled down peacefully to wait for the doctor to give her an injection and medicine.

Back home, the medicated oil scent was as usual, but seemed to have lost its pungency. From the kitchen came the sound of meat being chopped on a cutting board; from the hot pot rose the fragrance of rice porridge. The essence of life in this world needs no further explanation—it is simple and clear as that.

I often wonder, when I am ill and cooking porridge today, who is it for?

When I was little, it was mostly my father, sometimes my mother, who had the patience to 'chop beef' and cook porridge for me. This was a sick-day menu, and only I got to eat it. Sometimes, after seeing the doctor, I would pre-order this kind of meat porridge: 'I want spring onion and beef porridge.' That was the privilege of being ill. Now, no one will ever cook this particular porridge for me again; when I fall ill, I will never eat this kind of beef porridge anymore.

'When you're sick these days, just call Foodpanda,' a friend said. Some friends cook plain porridge or fish porridge for their wives. 'Sometimes I cook minced meat porridge.' 'I chop it by hand, not with a blender.' 'Just a few minutes and it's done.' Because a pot of porridge makes a person feel cherished.

'In a lifetime, not many people will cook porridge for you when you are ill. After growing up, the most likely scenario is that you cook it for others. These things, everyone has gone through them. No matter what you think, say a proper goodbye, speak from your heart—those reading it will feel comforted for you.' I told the student. She looked at me, a glint of light flashing in her eyes.

A piece about grandmother can bring consolation. My father, my mother, my grandmother… these are the stories we naturally know how to write.

The student is not simply a good writer; she seized on the medicated oil as the central thread, and around it conveyed her true feelings toward her closest kin. She may not have been grandmother's favourite, but that time together, arranged by fate, means she can never forget everything grandmother did for her, nor fail to understand that people simply grow up in such unknowing ways. In the end, she handed in a piece that was deeply moving and made one feel 'uncomfortable' in the most poignant sense.

The medicated oil went from being detestable, to dependable, to shameful, to a cherished memory. It turns out that on the first day the girl started primary school, she was laughed at by classmates for smelling of medicated oil and being a country bumpkin. She ran home crying, and angrily ordered her grandmother to use plenty of washing powder to wash every single piece of clothing from top to bottom; grandmother hugged the clothes and cried. Grandmother had been raising her since she was eight months old, until she grew up and went to school. Once the granddaughter came into contact with the outside world, she became like a different person—and broke grandmother's heart. After returning to live with her mother, one day grandmother had already developed dementia (Alzheimer's disease). The girl went back with her mother to visit, only to discover she was no longer 'recognised'.

'You can't be my granddaughter—she doesn't like talking to me.' The old grandmother said to the girl.

Life is both real and cruel. Have I ever been this cruel to my mother? Perhaps not. Or perhaps I have—just as unknowing as that girl. Family members sometimes hurt each other. What matters is, afterwards, have we come to understand love more deeply?
